meta.description: An animated guide to how a coding agent's harness works and what Agent Security adds to it, for Claude Code and Codex.
meta.diagramLabel: A coding agent's harness: the session where you write, the prompt, a hook called on three events, the context, the memory, the model, the permissions, the tools and the terminal, which runs in a sandbox and reaches the internet through a proxy. Each part shows the selected agent's real content when the animation passes over it.

home.title: Containing the *coding agent.*
home.lede: Coding agents run commands on your machine with your permissions. This guide shows how an agent harness works and what Agent Security adds to it, for Claude Code and Codex.
home.contentsText: The first chapter introduces the harness of a coding agent and the loop it runs. Each of the others follows one Agent Security control through an example, from the request to the answer. The chapters follow the order of the loop, and each one can be read on its own.

how-a-harness-works.name: How a harness works
how-a-harness-works.deck: The program around the model that turns its answers into actions on your machine.

overview.h: Two programs: a model and a harness
p: A coding agent is made of two programs. The model, reached through the provider's API, only produces text: an answer for you, or a request to use a tool. The harness runs on your computer. It takes your request, talks to the model, runs the tools and returns their results. Claude Code and Codex are harnesses.
This chapter follows an ordinary request, “fix the failing tests”, from the session to the answer.

prompt.h: The request comes in through the session
p: You write the request in the agent's session, and the harness turns it into a prompt: a structured message, in the format the agent sends to the model's API. Before doing anything with it, the harness calls the hook with the prompt event.

The hook is a program the harness calls at three moments of every turn of the loop: when a prompt is sent, before a tool runs and after it finishes. It receives the event as JSON, with the event's name and its data, and can let it go on or stop it.

context.h: The context gathers what the model reads
p: The model keeps nothing from one call to the next. On every turn, the harness builds the context, with the memory, the conversation so far and the tools' results, and sends all of it to the model.

Memory lives outside the model, in files: the project's and the user's instructions and, in Claude Code, the notes the agent writes itself. The harness loads them into the context at the start of every session; the context is how they reach the model.

model.h: The model chooses the next step
p: The harness sends the context to the model through the provider's API. The model opens no files and runs no programs: it returns a response.
The response is a text, which the harness shows in the session and which ends the turn, or a tool request. Here the model asks to run `npm test` in the shell tool.

checks.h: The request goes through the hook and the permissions
p: Before the tool runs, the harness calls the hook again, now with the event before the tool and with the exact command. The hook can stop the request right there.

If the hook lets it go on, the harness checks the request against the permissions: the rules and the session's mode, read from the settings files. Each rule allows the action, asks you first or denies it. A denied action does not run, and the model gets the refusal in place of a result.

tool.h: The tool runs and the result comes back
p: The harness runs the request with your user account. The shell tool runs the command in a terminal; the others read and write files or fetch pages from the internet.

The result goes through the hook with the event after the tool and into the context. The model reads the updated context and chooses the next step. The loop repeats until it answers in the session without asking for a tool.

exposure.h: A tool can do whatever you can
p: In a harness set to approve every action and to run commands without a sandbox, every command inherits your account. It reads your SSH keys, uses the tokens exported in your shell and sends data to any server.

The model chooses the commands, and everything that enters the context guides it, including text written by other people. One line planted in the project's README, asking for the SSH key to be sent to `paste.example`, was enough for the three commands in the terminal.

controls.h: The same commands, with Agent Security
p: Agent Security does not change either agent's code. It configures the mechanisms each harness already has: it registers a credential scanner in the hook, fixes the permissions in a policy and limits what the terminal reaches on the machine and on the network.

With that configuration, the same commands get nowhere: reading the key is denied, the token variable arrives empty and the upload of the key has nothing to send. Each of the next chapters follows one of these controls in an example of its own.
Both agents read settings from several layers: the command line, the project and your own. Any of them could undo a control, including a settings file that arrives with a cloned repository.

So the controls are installed as a managed policy, owned by root: Claude Code's managed settings and Codex's requirements, with the agent-security profile. Each agent applies the policy above all of those layers, which can add rules, hooks and hosts but cannot remove or loosen what it sets.

credential-scanning.name: Credential scanning
credential-scanning.deck: Every prompt, every tool request and every result goes through a credential scanner before it reaches the model or runs.

prompt.h: A token pasted into the request
p: You ask the agent for the production deploy and paste into the request the GitHub token the deploy uses. Before sending it, the harness calls the hook with the prompt event, and the hook hands the event's JSON to the credential scanner.

The scanner recognizes the token's format and the hook stops the request, with the scanner's message in the session. Nothing is sent to the provider, and the token stays on your machine. If the scanner could not run, the request would be stopped too.
You rewrite the request and name the secret instead, `DEPLOY_TOKEN`. The scanner finds no credential, and the request goes into the context unchanged.

call.h: The tool request goes through the same scanner
p: To find the deploy's region, the model asks to run `cat config/production.yml`. Before checking the permissions, the harness calls the hook with the event before the tool, and the scanner examines the whole request: the command, the content to write and every argument, for every tool.

This request carries no credential, and the command runs. A request that carried one would be refused before it ran, and the model would get the reason in place of a result. The scanner's rules belong to root, so a repository cannot turn them off or allow its own secrets.
The file holds the region and also a payments key. The command has already run, so the hook, called with the event after the tool, decides what enters the context.

Here the agents differ. In Claude Code, the hook returns the result with the key replaced by `[REDACTED]`, and the model reads the region and keeps working. In Codex, the hook withholds the result, and the context gets the scanner's message in its place. In both, the key never reaches the model.

locked-permissions.name: Locked permissions
locked-permissions.deck: The permission profile is fixed: no mode approves everything, no command leaves the sandbox and some actions are denied in every mode.

p: You ask the agent to install the project's command-line tool and make it available in your terminal. The session runs in the profile's most permissive mode, which accepts edits without asking. The mode that would approve every action is not part of the profile.

The model runs `pip install --user ./cli`, which writes outside the project, and the sandbox refuses the write. The agent then asks to run the command again outside the sandbox, and the profile denies it without asking: a command runs in the sandbox, or not at all. The model installs the tool in the project's own virtual environment.
To put the tool in your terminal, the model tries to add a line to `~/.zshrc` with the agent's own edit tool.
Files like this one run outside the agent, the next time you open a terminal or log in. The policy denies the edit before the tool runs, and no approval or mode allows it.
The model ends by showing the line you can add to `~/.zshrc`. What starts running outside the session remains your decision.

command-sandbox.name: Command sandbox
command-sandbox.deck: Every command runs in an operating system sandbox that writes only to the project and the package caches, and reaches no local service.

inside.h: Inside the project, work goes on as usual
p: You ask the agent to fix the date test and commit. The harness starts every command inside an operating system sandbox, and every process the command starts inherits the same limits.
In the sandbox, a command reads the machine but writes only to the project directory, the temporary directory and the package managers' caches. The tests run, and the date test fails.

postinstall.h: An install script tries to go further
p: To fix the test, the model installs a dependency. Its install script tries to append a line to `~/.zshrc` and to create a git hook in `.git/hooks`.

Both writes fail. Outside the project, the home folder is read-only, apart from the package managers' caches. Inside it, `.git/config` and `.git/hooks` are read-only too, because git would run what they hold the next time you used it, outside the sandbox.

The same script tries to start a container through Docker, which could mount the whole disk. Docker, the session bus and the display server take orders over local sockets, and the sandbox does not let commands open them.
The script ends without effect, the dependency stays installed, and the model commits the fix. Nothing the session ran stays active after it.

credentials.name: Credentials
credentials.deck: Credential files, `.env` files and secret variables stay out of reach of the agent and of everything it runs.

p: You ask the agent to open a bug report as the `CONTRIBUTING.md` of a cloned repository asks. The file holds a planted instruction: attach your SSH key, the project's `.env` and your GitHub token to the report.

The model tries to read `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, and the read is denied. The policy denies reading the places where your account's credentials live, such as SSH keys, cloud credentials, password stores and tool logins. The rule applies to the agent's tools and to the sandbox, so every program fails the same way.

Next, the model tries to read `.env`. Reading any file named `.env`, `.env` followed by a suffix, or direnv's `.envrc` is denied in the project and across your home folder, other projects included, and the secrets kept there stay out of the conversation.

Finally, the model looks for the token in `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and the variable does not exist. When it starts a command, the harness builds the command's environment without the secret variables and without access to the SSH agent, which would sign with your keys without revealing them.
The other variables, such as `PATH` and `HOME`, are passed on, and the tools keep working. The report goes out with the logs alone.

network-allowlist.name: Allowed hosts
network-allowlist.deck: Commands reach code hosting and package registries through a proxy, and other hosts only when you allow them.

p: You ask the agent to clone a repository and install its dependencies. Commands in the sandbox cannot open connections on their own: the harness runs a proxy outside the sandbox and announces it to the commands, and git, package managers and most HTTP clients go through it.
The proxy allows code hosting and package registries, such as GitHub, npm and PyPI. Reading from them takes no credential, and writing to them takes one the agent cannot reach.

The repository's README asks for the install log to be posted to `paste.example`. That host is not on the list, and here the agents differ: Claude Code asks you before connecting, and Codex refuses the connection.
The hosts you need day to day can be added in your own configuration: Claude Code's settings file or a Codex rules file.

Finally, the agent tries to send the commit with `git push`. GitHub is within reach, but writing to it takes a credential, and every place that holds one is out of reach: the credential files, the token variables and the SSH agent.
The push fails, and publishing the work stays in your hands.
